title: Degree And Lefschetz Number
notes: Open by naming the lecture's conversion rule: homology turns maps into small algebraic numbers, and those numbers can force geometry. The source span moves from degree through Euler-Poincare and Borsuk-Ulam into Lefschetz fixed points and dimension by nerves, so present the deck as one chain of detectors rather than a list of isolated theorems.

title: Degree As Top Homology Multiplier
notes: Emphasize that degree is not first a picture of winding; it is the integer multiplying the top homology generator. The winding picture is a model students can inspect. Once the class in top homology is fixed, homotopic maps cannot change the multiplier, which is why degree becomes an obstruction.

title: Lifts Make Degree Visible
notes: Use the lift plots to make the integer measurable. A circle-valued map can be followed upstairs on the real line, and the endpoint displacement divided by one full turn gives the degree. Ask students to compare the positive, negative, and zero slopes before naming the four entries.

title: Composition Multiplies Degree
notes: Frame the interactive artifact as a check on functoriality. The induced map of a composite is the composite of induced maps, so top homology multipliers multiply. The displayed sample, degree three followed by degree negative two, gives degree negative six and prevents an additive misconception.

title: Chains Before Homology
notes: Pause on the distinction between chain data and homology data. The reflection visibly permutes vertices and oriented edges, but the useful survivor is the action on the loop generator in H1. This example also prepares the Hopf trace theorem by showing traces before and after passing to homology.

title: Euler-Poincare Ledger
notes: Treat the ledger as a bookkeeping theorem with teeth. The left side counts cells in alternating dimensions, while the right side counts homology dimensions. The agreement across a point, a circle, a disk, a sphere boundary, and a figure eight makes Euler characteristic feel computable and homotopy-aware.

title: Mod-2 Chains And Parity
notes: Introduce mod-2 homology as the place where orientation signs disappear but parity remains meaningful. This is the correct language for antipodal arguments because paired cells cancel in twos. Students should hear that the chapter is not abandoning integral degree, but adding a parity detector for symmetry.

title: Borsuk-Ulam Gap
notes: Make the one-dimensional Borsuk-Ulam witness concrete. The two sampled curves are values at antipodal inputs, and the gap reverses sign after the antipodal move. A continuous sign-reversing gap must vanish, so the vertical red pair marks equal values rather than a numerical accident.

title: Antipodal Obstruction
notes: Connect the gap plot back to the homological proof strategy. If every antipodal pair had different values, one normalizes the difference and obtains an odd map to a lower sphere. Mod-2 degree rules out the needed factorization, giving the obstruction behind the visible zero.

title: Lefschetz Number
notes: Define the Lefschetz number as an alternating trace, not as a fixed-point count. For a compact triangulable space, a nonzero value forces at least one fixed point. The formula for S1, Lambda equals one minus degree, lets students reuse the degree intuition immediately.

title: Reflection Forces Fixed Points
notes: Use reflection as the clean test case. The map has degree negative one on the circle, so Lambda is two, and the artifact marks two fixed points with positive local index. The important conclusion is existence from trace data; the picture helps locate witnesses after the theorem has already forced them.

title: Hopf Trace
notes: Explain Hopf trace as the bridge that makes Lefschetz calculable from finite models. Alternating traces on chain groups equal alternating traces on homology, even though individual chain traces depend on the chosen triangulation. That equality is why a matrix calculation can support a topological fixed-point theorem.

title: Sphere Degree Lab
notes: Read the table as a decision engine. Given a sphere dimension and a degree, the formula returns the Lefschetz number and therefore whether this invariant forces a fixed point. Stress the silent cases: Lambda equal zero does not prove absence of fixed points; it only says this detector has no signal.

title: Proof Dependency Map
notes: Use the dependency map to show how the chapter's named ideas feed one another. Degree and rational traces lead into Lefschetz; mod-2 chains feed antipodal arguments; open-cover nerves support dimension. The visual also gives students a way to review the chapter without following the original page order.

title: Dimension By Nerves
notes: Slow down the word refinement. A single cover can have an overlarge nerve because all sets overlap at once, so dimension is not read from one convenient cover. The refined cover lowers the nerve to dimension one, matching the circle and showing why the definition quantifies over refinements.

title: Invariant Recap
notes: Close by asking what each invariant is allowed to see. Degree sees top-dimensional orientation behavior, Euler characteristic sees alternating homology size, Borsuk-Ulam sees antipodal parity, Lefschetz sees fixed-point pressure, and nerve dimension sees how covers can be refined. This recap ties the computational artifacts back to the chapter's proof logic.
